title: OXO: Why Change the Peeler Handle First in 1990? | Brand Stories
description:
What must change in a peeler handle to take it from impossible to hold to something another pair of hands can try?

Follow OXO through clay, prototypes, a rejected smooth bubble design, materials and connections, then trade-show samples, a shop trial and one named author's account of family use.

The origins and early process follow retrospective accounts by the brand, named designers and museums. A patent describes proposals; a museum prototype is not the first production model's bill of materials. Shop reactions are recollections, and the family trial is Lauralee Alben's personal account, not evidence of general therapeutic benefits. 1997 is the publication year, not a confirmed trial date. Anonymous images are conceptual illustrations.

thumbnail.headline:
How Do You Peel
If You Cannot Grip?

chapters.c10r1-h01: Opening: Get a Grip on This Peeler
chapters.c10r1-r01: Fingers Wrap Around, the Direction Stays
chapters.c10r1-m01: Finger Pads Press, Fins Give Way
chapters.c10r1-a01: Connect the Blade, Deliver the Samples
chapters.c10r5-s01: Try It, Then Hand It to Someone Else

c10h01.text: If you cannot even hold a peeler, how will you make dinner?

c10h02.text: The OXO peeler in MoMA's collection is only 17.8 centimeters long. The hard part is making it something your hand can hold.

c10h03.text: Go back in time and imagine a kitchen in Provence, with your fingers pinching a thin, rigid metal handle.

c10h04.text: You have not started peeling, yet your fingers are already struggling to close around it.

c10h05.text: First, I want to see where those hands can actually fit.

c10h06.text: On a table, a lump of clay waits to be shaped.

c10h07.text: On another table, an unfamiliar black handle waits for someone to reach out.

c10h08.text: Today, follow OXO and a peeler's journey from hard to hold to ready for someone else to try.

c10h09.text: When a different hand picks it up, what exactly must change about the handle?

c10o01.text: The hands that struggled to close belonged to Betsey Farber. The brand's retrospective says she had mild arthritis.

c10o02.text: That kind of metal peeler was difficult for her to hold while cooking.

c10o03.text: Betsey was an architect. Her husband Sam had just retired from the kitchenware company he founded.

c10o04.text: The museum notes that the couple enjoyed cooking and art in Provence, but this little tool caused trouble.

c10o05.text: Could a moldable material first change the part she had to hold?

c10o06.text: Designer Davin Stowell later recalled that Betsey molded clay around the metal peeler.

c10o07.text: She was looking for a shape that felt more comfortable to hold.

c10o08.text: Imagine holding it yourself now. As your fingers push the clay, the thin handle gains an adjustable layer of thickness.

c10o09.text: Let go and look at the indentations. You can reshape the side that does not fit your hand.

c10o11.text: I want to know whose hands first tried the prototypes.

c10o12a.text: Stowell recalled Sam insisting that this could not be a special tool made just for a small group.

c10o12b.text: He was talking about a business reality: a tiny market would struggle to support the product.

c10o13.text: Sam approached Smart Design in New York. To change existing kitchenware, do you first ask people who cook or people who struggle to use their hands?

c10o14.text: The museum's research says the team spoke to consumers and chefs, and asked arthritis groups in New York about their difficulties.

c10o15.text: Team member Dan Formosa later noted that professional chefs could have arthritis too.

c10o16.text: They also examined existing kitchen tools, finding rusted metal, cracked plastic and uncomfortable handles.

c10o17.text: Your turn: pick up the tool and change direction. Can this handle follow your movement?

c10v5o02.text: An interview about the early designs says the team grouped kitchen tools by hand and wrist movements. Where did the peeler belong?

c10v5o03.text: The peeler's movements were pushing and pulling. Pick it up and try moving your hand forward, then back.

c10o19.text: A later design catalogue shows wood, rubber, plastic and foam among the materials used for handle prototypes.

c10o20.text: The team made dozens of different models to explore on the table.

c10v5o01.text: The museum also notes that different prototypes went to chefs, ordinary users and arthritis groups in New York for trials.

c10o22.text: Next, the handle they would actually hand over had to let fingers wrap back around it.

c10r01.text: The museum collection still holds a wooden grip study with four raised areas on its handle.

c10r02.text: Another peeler handle, made from foam and plastic, still has a cylindrical outline.

c10r03.text: Imagine picking one up from the table, turning it slightly in your palm, then trying the next.

c10r05.text: Stowell said that handles were hard to grip if they were too large or too thin.

c10r08.text: Beyond size, the blade's direction also depends on the part you hold.

c10r09.text: Imagine turning your wrist along a vegetable's curved surface. The blade must still point where you want it to go.

c10r10.text: If the handle spins in your palm, can you keep the blade at the same angle?

c10r11.text: Stowell said an oval handle was less likely to rotate and gave the hand a useful sense of direction.

c10r13.text: The moment you turn your wrist interests me most.

c10r14.text: Imagine wrapping your palm around the wider side, then bringing your fingers back around from the side.

c10r16.text: Once your fingers meet the outline, how should the surface receive their pads?

c10v5b01.text: Stowell discussed another early idea: deformable bubbles hidden beneath a smooth handle surface.

c10v5b02.text: His idea was that sometimes a hand grips tightly and pulls, and sometimes it pulls gently. The handle needed to adapt to the grip.

c10v5b03.text: But those preliminary designs were abandoned. Stowell said they did not intuitively show people what they could do.

c10v5b05.text: I wonder how, on first touching that smooth surface, you would know where you could squeeze.

c10r18.text: Stowell remembered a piece of bicycle grip nearby as he talked with Sam.

c10r19.text: It had thin little fins that deformed when pinched between thumb and forefinger.

c10r21.text: When you hold this little tool, could those two fingers also find a place that gives under pressure?

c10m01.text: In a handle patent filed in 1990, Stowell and his colleague Michael Callahan drew recessed areas on both sides.

c10m01a.text: The recesses are themselves oval and extend along the handle. The document says they align with the pads of the thumb and forefinger.

c10m02.text: Each side has a row of little fins, with spaces between them.

c10m03.text: In the drawing, the thumb and forefinger press against the sides, deforming the fins into a yielding contact area.

c10m05.text: I want to squeeze that spot myself and try it.

c10m06.text: For these details to actually bend, what material should they choose?

c10m08.text: Museum records identify the early peeler's handle as Santoprene, a thermoplastic rubber.

c10m09.text: A materials catalogue says this range's handles were injection-molded, with the material selected for softness, a warm feel and durability.

c10m10a.text: Surprisingly, the brand's retrospective traces the material search into industrial uses, such as seals inside equipment.

c10m11.text: Imagine the material as pellets before molding, then look at the little fins you can press down. Those details must be formed as part of the shape.

c10m13.text: Yet when you actually cook, your hands may also be wet.

c10m14.text: The brand's retrospective says they also chose this thermoplastic rubber for its resistance to slipping when wet.

c10m15.text: Imagine picking the peeler up again just after washing vegetables.

c10m17.text: The brand also says it combines well with kitchenware materials such as stainless steel and can withstand dishwasher use.

c10m18.text: You finish peeling, wash the tool and return it to the drawer.

c10m19.text: But when you hold a soft handle, how does it carry the blade's direction through?

c10a01.text: That handle patent draws an internal cavity extending lengthwise into the handle.

c10a02.text: The tool's shank enters the cavity, its dimensions fitting so the outer handle surrounds it.

c10a03.text: Imagine one hand holding the hollow, soft handle while the other pushes the rigid connecting part inside.

c10a05.text: Unexpectedly, the document first uses a brush to illustrate the structure, while also listing peelers among the tools it can apply to.

c10a07.text: I worry about the moment you pull back. Could only the soft handle remain in your hand, with the tool left behind?

c10a08.text: One proposal in the document places the shank's enlarged head against the handle's end, then secures it with adhesive.

c10a10.text: If the connection does not rely on that adhesive, what else could the shank's shape do?

c10a11.text: The authors also draw a shank with different thicknesses above and below, forming a step. The cavity has a matching step.

c10a12.text: When those two parts align, the structure resists the handle being pulled off.

c10a15.text: Besides hanging it up, where else could your fingers go in that large hole at the end?

c10a16.text: The patent describes inserting the thumb and forefinger into the openings on either side, pinching the handle's end to pull the tool when needed.

c10a18.text: When you hang it back up, could the shape of the opening help too?

c10a18x.text: The document shapes the opening wider at both sides and narrower toward the middle.

c10a18a.text: The authors say this entrance makes it easier for people with unsteady hands and poor vision to align the hole with a support hook.

c10a18b.text: Imagine bringing the handle toward the hook, letting the opening meet it first, then letting the hook pass through.

c10v5p01.text: Another museum peeler prototype brings the question to the blade: what holds it in place?

c10v5p02.text: The blade is a pivoting metal strip, with one hole at the top and another at the bottom of its support.

c10v5p03.text: Two attachment points sit in those two holes.

c10v5f01.text: To get this tool into other hands, could they find a factory willing to make it?

c10v5f02.text: In a later PBS interview, Stowell recalled that with only two months until the planned trade-show debut, a manufacturer had still not been chosen.

c10v5f03.text: Sam remembered a Japanese manufacturer he had worked with in his earlier kitchenware business.

c10v5f04.text: They visited the factory and received the answer: yes, they would make it.

c10v5f05.text: Hearing that, I start watching the trade show's opening date. If you were waiting for samples, how late could you wait?

c10v5f06.text: Two days before the show opened, a box arrived.

c10v5f07.text: He said it contained samples, which he described as perfect.

c10v5f08.text: He remembered the show opening in May 1990.

c10v5f09.text: If you stocked these tools in your shop, would customers simply reach for them?

c10v5s01.text: Stowell named the housewares retailer Lechters as buying the whole product line.

c10v5s02.text: But he recalled that sales were slower than the retailer had expected.

c10v5s03.text: Sam's idea was to put out a bowl of carrots first.

c10v5s04.text: Here is the black-handle trial teased at the start: a peeler chained to a bowl of carrots, inviting shoppers to try it.

c10l06.text: Imagine walking to the table and picking it up, your fingers settling on the handle before the blade touches the food.

c10l07.text: Your hand moves forward and the blade starts working.

c10v5s05.text: Unexpectedly, in his recollection, sales picked up quickly after customers could try peeling.

c10v5s06.text: A later article about the design also noted packaging that left the handle exposed.

c10v5s07.text: Before buying, customers could reach out, touch it and give it a squeeze.

c10v5u01.text: In an article published in 1997, design writer Alben described using it herself. What did she try first?

c10v5u02.text: She bought one and peeled carrots with it. She said she enjoyed using it.

c10v5u03.text: She then took the peeler to her husband's parents, Jim and Paula, for them to try.

c10v5u04.text: She recorded their first reactions: comfortable, a big black handle that was easy to hold, and less need to squeeze hard.

c10v5u06.text: What about you? Would you just hold it, or actually fetch a potato?

c10v5u07.text: Alben wrote that they took turns peeling potatoes with it.

c10v5u08.text: She also recorded them saying that the blade was sharp and worked when peeling toward themselves or away.

c10v5u09.text: Reading this, I find myself waiting to see how they will put it away.

c10v5u10.text: In the article, they then said: let's try hanging it up.

c10v5u11.text: The next response was: yes, that works too.

c10v5u12.text: Then the two of them brought out their original metal peeler.

c10v5u13.text: They held the new and old peelers side by side.

c10v5u14.text: Finally, they threw the old one into the trash.

c10l19.text: My answer is this: to pass a tool to another pair of hands, its handle must first make room for people to control it themselves.

c10l20.text: Tell me in the comments which small tool at home you would give a new handle, and which movement is hardest on your hand.

c10l21.text: Subscribe to the channel to keep exploring how design changes the things you do every day.
